article.Citation: Anderson T, et al. Psychedelic microdosing benefits and challenges: an empirical codebook. Harm Reduction Journal. 2019.
article.Title: Psychedelic microdosing benefits and challenges: an empirical codebook

ae_events.Description: Physical symptoms: disrupted vision, temperature dysregulation, numbness/tingling, insomnia, GI distress, reduced appetite, increased migraines/headaches (18.0%, 108.5 reports).
Impaired focus: poor concentration, distractibility, absent-mindedness reported by microdosers (8.8%, 53 of 603.5 coded challenge reports).
Increased anxiety (general, social, existential) reported as a microdosing drawback (6.7%, 40.5 of 603.5 coded challenge reports).
Impaired energy: restlessness/jitters (excess) or fatigue/drowsiness/brain fog (inadequate) reported (7.2%, 43.5 of 603.5 coded challenge reports).
Impaired mood: sadness, discontent, irritability, mood swings, fear, feeling unusual reported as a drawback (6.9%, 41.5 of 603.5 reports).
Social interference: awkwardness, oversharing, difficulty with sentence production in social settings (2.6%, 15.5 of 603.5 coded reports).
Cognitive interference: confusion, disorientation, racing thoughts, poor memory reported as a challenge (2.3%, 14 of 603.5 coded reports).
Self-interference: dissociation, depersonalization, rumination/over-analysis reported as a challenge (1.2%, 7.5 of 603.5 coded reports).
Increased symptoms: concerns re: psychological dependence/addiction potential, substance tolerance, comedown/hangover after effects (part of 6.2%, 37.5 reports).
Rare "adverse psychological events" noted by authors within increased-symptoms category; no further detail given (0.7% of coded challenges).

article.PosResult: The article has no single primary outcome to assess against; its own core finding is 'emergent parallelism'—nearly every domain (mood, self-efficacy, focus, energy, cognition, anxiety, physiology) was reported as both a benefit and a matched challenge by respondents (e.g., 92.9% improved mood vs. 41.5 challenge-reports of impaired mood; 18.0% physiological discomfort vs. 3.0% physiological enhancement), and the Discussion explicitly frames results as exploratory/inconclusive rather than net-positive or net-negative, so directionality is coded Indeterminate.
article.IsObservational: Explicitly a 'cross-sectional, retrospective, anonymous online survey' of 278 microdosers with no experimental manipulation; Discussion states 'this study was observational, not experimental.' It is a primary study with its own participant sample (N=278), not merely a methods/codebook-development paper without a patient population — the codebook is a data-analytic product built FROM this study's own survey respondents, so all extractable fields are populated from this sample.
article.Condition: Study population is a general community sample of psychedelic microdosers (LSD/psilocybin users recruited via Reddit), not selected on the basis of alcohol, smoking, or opioid use disorder. Reduced alcohol/tobacco use appears only as a secondary self-reported behavioral outcome for a subset, not as an inclusion criterion or study focus, so none of Alcohol/Smoking/Opioid applies; coded '.'.
article.N: 278 is the final analyzed sample ('The sample analysed in the present study includes the 278 respondents that answered the MDBC questions'), broken into LSD-only (195), psilocybin-only (50), and both (33).
article.AE_denominator: Challenge/AE-type reports are presented as % of 603.5 total coded challenge units, not as counts of participants who reported >=1 challenge. A subjective-importance-of-challenges analysis cites only partial subgroup counts (N1=177 LSD-only, N2=46 psilocybin-only) that don't sum to a clean total, so the exact number of respondents contributing >=1 challenge cannot be determined; coded 'Not numbered' since the concept (challenges assessed over some subset of the 278) clearly applies.
article.ArmScope: This is a single-group observational survey with no non-psychedelic comparator arm — all 278 respondents were psychedelic microdosers. The arm-based 'psychedelic_arm' vs 'pooled' distinction (built for multi-arm trial designs) doesn't cleanly apply, so coded 'NA'.
article.PctFemale: 31/278 = 11.2% female, from 'Most participants were male (M 237, F 31, other 10)'.
article.GenderCategory: Preserves the reported 3-category breakdown (male/female/other) including the 'other' n=10 so it is not lost by collapsing to a binary %female.
article.PctBIPOC: Derived as (278-234)/278 = 44/278 = 15.8% from 'white or European (N = 234, other 44)'; 'other' here is used as the non-white/European category.
article.PctIndigenous: Not broken out anywhere in the text as a distinct subgroup of the 'other' 44 respondents; coded '.'.
article.NumDistinctAEs: The challenges taxonomy has 11 top-level categories (44 lowest-level codes, mostly without individual stats). Of the 11 categories, 'Illegality' (29.5%) was excluded as a socio-legal/economic circumstance the authors themselves state is 'not an outcome of microdosing per se', not a health/psychological AE. 'Other perceived challenges' (10.6%) was excluded as an incoherent catch-all mixing 'no challenges reported' counter-responses, logistical concerns (remembering to dose), and misc. substance-related notes, with no single describable event. The remaining 9 categories were extracted as AE01-AE09; the 'Increased symptoms (other)' category (6.2%) was further split into AE09 (dependence/tolerance/comedown concerns) and AE10 (the explicitly author-labeled 'adverse psychological events, 0.7%') because the latter is uniquely flagged by the authors as clinically concerning and merits separate tracking. Total = 10.
article.NParticipantsWithAE: All frequencies in the article are report-level (out of 603.5 total coded challenge reports, respondents could submit up to 3), not participant-level counts of who had >=1 challenge; no figure convertible to participants-with-AE is given.
article.WorstSeverity: All 10 extracted events default to Mild per the severity rubric (no intervention, persistence, or FDA-seriousness signal is reported for any category), so max severity across ae_events is Mild.

ae_events.Anderson 2019_AE01: Grouped physiological-discomfort sub-codes (vision disruption, temp dysregulation, numbness/tingling, insomnia, GI distress, appetite loss, headaches) as reported by the article; no per-symptom severity, duration, or intervention detail given, so graded Mild/indeterminate per the rubric's under-specified-AE default. Onset 'unknown' because this reflects an ongoing microdosing regimen (repeated low doses over time), not a single identifiable dosing session.
ae_events.Anderson 2019_AE02: No duration, functional-impairment persistence, or intervention detail beyond the category label 'impaired focus'; defaulted Mild/indeterminate per rubric.
ae_events.Anderson 2019_AE03: Coded as 'challenging_experience' (CEQ-adjacent anxiety phenomenology) per the rubric's explicit guidance that in-session-type anxiety should be flagged this way rather than folded into a generic AE count; no intervention/persistence detail given so Mild/indeterminate by rubric default (a high subjective anxiety report alone does not escalate above Mild).
ae_events.Anderson 2019_AE04: No detail on which pole (restlessness vs fatigue) predominated per respondent, nor duration/intervention; defaulted Mild/indeterminate.
ae_events.Anderson 2019_AE05: No detail on duration beyond the acute period or intervention; defaulted Mild/indeterminate despite inclusion of 'fear' descriptor, since no escalation signal (intervention, persistence, seriousness) is given.
ae_events.Anderson 2019_AE08: Includes dissociation/depersonalization, which could plausibly be graded higher with more detail, but the article gives no duration, functional-impairment, or intervention information, so per the rubric's explicit instruction not to default ungradeable events to Severe, graded Mild/indeterminate.
ae_events.Anderson 2019_AE09: Distinguishes generic dependence/tolerance/comedown concerns (this row) from the explicitly author-flagged 'adverse psychological events' (AE10); no severity-relevant detail given for this sub-component, so Mild/indeterminate.
ae_events.Anderson 2019_AE10: The article itself calls these 'more concerning, but rare, adverse psychological events (0.7%)' with zero further description (no named events, no intervention, no outcome). Per the rubric's explicit instruction that under-specified AEs default to Mild (to avoid overstating harm as much as under-reporting it), and that qualitative author concern language alone is not a seriousness signal, this is graded Mild but flagged SeverityIndeterminate='Y' — a human reviewer should note this is the single event in this article most likely to be underweighted by that default and may warrant the source dataset (osf.io/g5cwy/) being consulted for detail.
